job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Tomas Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Tomas, and thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live above my parents' hardware shop in Marsden, and I'm downstairs by eight to help with deliveries and the books. My father still writes receipts by hand, so I keep a ledger in a notebook for him and put it in the computer at night. I went to the regional university for accounting and passed with an average result, no internship, because I worked at the shop in the holidays. For six months I've been applying to small accounting practices and I go to Mass on Sundays, which keeps me steady. I'd like a job where I learn a trade properly under a person who knows it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, nothing changes, and people get on with honest work. I'd tell friends not to chase every new gadget. I don't post online, so I'd say it over a coffee after Mass.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm still worried, because I'm a pass-degree graduate with no offer and a loan, and AI hype didn't cause that. What I need is someone to give me a chance and show me the work. In a world where nothing changes, I'd still need that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying to small practices in town, ten a week, and I'd visit three in person with my CV, because a handshake counts. I'd keep the shop books and offer to do local people's tax forms for a small fee. I'd stay at home and pay my parents a bit toward the utilities.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, with some worry. I trust people more than machines and I'm glad nothing is changing there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do in the shop that an accounting firm would value?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know how a small business lives week to week: stock, credit, what a customer owes. I've chased unpaid invoices from builders who then bought nails from us the next week. A firm that serves small businesses would value that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your family has the most say about your next step?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father, mostly, and the parish priest, who knows half the town. My father says go and learn under a good man, not a big name. My mother says stay close until you have something solid.

I'd tell friends not to chase every new **gadget**.
think: I'm still worried about being a **pass-degree** graduate with no offer and a loan.
I need someone to give me a **chance** and show me the work.

Keep the shop books and offer local **tax forms** for a small fee.
feel: **Steady**, with some worry, trusting people more than machines.

fieldNote: His **worry** is the missing first job and the loan, not the technology.

steps.text: Visit three small accounting practices a week with a printed CV
Offer local people a tax-form service for a small fee
Keep the shop's books and deliveries going

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is why trades and apprenticeships matter. People who can do real work with their hands and their word will be fine. I'd say let companies train their own people instead of waiting for the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm worried, because the small practices I'm applying to will use software for data entry, checking and the basic accounts. I'm slow with new tools and I've never used AI. A practice that needs four juniors may take one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a practice asked, I'd learn the accounting software, since that's just a better ledger. I'd stay away from the rest unless I had to. I'd also look at trades where my accounts skill helps, like a builder's firm or a farm supplier, who need someone to run the office. I'd stop going out on Fridays and put that into my loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I feel I'm being told to change the way I do things, and I don't like being rushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of the small practice's jobs would the software take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Data entry, bank checking and the first drafts of accounts. A person still sits across from a customer and says this is what you owe. I think that part stays human, for a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try any of the tools if a practice asked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a practice insisted, yes, one tool at a time and with someone showing me. I'd rather be slow and right than quick and wrong.

say: I'd say this is why **apprenticeships** matter, and companies should train their own people.
I'd say don't wait for the government.
think: Small practices will use software for **data entry** and basic accounts, so fewer juniors.
I'm slow with new tools and have **never** used AI.
do: Learn the practice's **accounting software**, which is just a better ledger.
Look at builders' firms and farm suppliers that need an **office** person and stop Friday outings.
feel: **Uneasy**, rushed into changing how I do things.
S1.quote: I'd rather be slow and right than quick and wrong.
fieldNote: His **resistance** softens only for tools that look like a better ledger.
He points to trades firms as a place where his skills matter.
He wants firms, not government, to train people.

steps.text: Learn the accounting software a small practice would use
Apply to builders' firms and farm suppliers that need an office person
Stop Friday evening outings and put the money toward the loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have to look after one another. The government and firms need to act quickly, but families and parishes will do the real work. I'd say hold on to what's solid, like faith, family and honest work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm afraid. An accounting degree is thinking work and it would be gone before I've had one year in a job. I'd have a loan and nothing to show, and I don't have the tools skills to compete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay put with my parents and work every hour at the shop, since hands-on work comes later. I'd cut every cost, stop the gym and the phone upgrade, and put what's left into savings. I'd ask the parish for advice and any local work, and I'd ask my father's suppliers if they need help with deliveries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and a bit angry. Everyone told us to study, and now study doesn't buy a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents and the people at church?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll face it together, as families always have. My father would nod and my mother would light a candle. Then we'd talk about how much the shop makes and what we'd need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What stays human if thinking work goes in two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hands and presence. Selling a nail and knowing the customer's name, fixing a gutter, making a delivery. I'd be a shopkeeper's son and glad of it.

say: I'd say we must **look after** one another, and families and parishes do the real work.
I'd tell people to hold on to what's solid.
think: An accounting degree is thinking work and could be **gone** within a year of a first job.
I have a loan and not the **tools skills** to compete.
do: Work every hour at the **shop**, since hands-on work comes later.
Cut every cost, put the rest in **savings** and ask the parish for local work.
feel: **Frightened** and a bit angry that study no longer buys a job.
S2.quote: Everyone told us to study, and now study doesn't buy a job.
fieldNote: Two years turns his **degree** into a loan with nothing to show.
His fallback is real: the family shop and its suppliers.
He leans on faith and family more than public programmes.

steps.text: Work full shifts at the family hardware shop
Stop the gym and cancel the phone upgrade
Put every spare coin into a savings account
Ask the parish about local work and advice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, so use it. Learn a trade, build something, keep your word. I'd tell friends to do what's in front of them and not to wait for rescue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm worried but not hopeless. I'd get at least a few years of experience before it arrives, and I could learn the basics of the new tools, slowly. But I'd keep a plan B in the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd find a small practice or a builder's office, learn from the owner and take every exam I'm allowed. I'd save a third of my pay, and I'd learn one tool at a time, starting with the accounting software. I'd stay close to my parents and keep the shop books so the family has something to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but steady. It's a long road, and long roads suit me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would five years let you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honesty, hard work, and how to deal with money. I'd say learn a skill with your hands as well as your head. The rest they can pick up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your own children to learn, if you have any one day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to prove myself. In two years I'm a boy with a certificate. In five I'm a man with references.

say: I'd say five years is a fair warning, so learn a **trade** and keep your word.
I'd tell friends not to wait for **rescue**.
think: I'm worried but not hopeless: a few years of **experience** before it arrives.
I'd keep a **plan B** in the shop.
do: Join a small practice or builder's office and take every **exam** I'm allowed.
Save a **third** of my pay and learn one tool at a time.
feel: **Anxious** but steady, since long roads suit me.
S3.quote: In two years I'm a boy with a certificate. In five I'm a man with references.
fieldNote: Five years gives him **time** to prove himself and gather references.
He keeps the shop as a plan B.
His values, honesty and hands as well as head, shape every choice.

steps.text: Join a small practice or builder's office and learn from the owner
Take every professional exam the employer allows
Save a third of every pay cheque
Keep the shop books so the family has a fallback

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so no need for noise. People should get on with learning and working. I'd say keep an eye on the young ones, so they aren't left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be fairly steady. I'd have time for a first job, a promotion, maybe a marriage and a house. I'd still worry about being the old man who didn't learn the new things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a first job in a small practice, qualify as an accountant, and move to running the office of a firm or the family shop. I'd save for a small house and probably marry. I'd learn each new tool when it proves itself, slowly but properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It's what I'd call a normal problem, like a long winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you do something differently about work and family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to marry, I'd say, and buy a house in Marsden. I'd want my own children to grow up with grandparents nearby, as I did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you even with that much time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being left behind by my own habits. I'm slow with machines and I know it. Ten years would force me to change, and I'd have to be humble about it.

say: I'd say ten years is plenty, so **no noise**, just get on with learning and working.
I'd say watch the **young ones** so they aren't left behind.
think: I'd be fairly **steady**, with time for a job, a promotion and maybe a marriage.
I worry about being the old man who didn't **learn**.

S4.quote: I'm slow with machines and I know it. Ten years would force me to change, and I'd have to be humble about it.
fieldNote: With a **decade** he feels steady, yet his own slowness is the worry he names.

steps.text: Get a first job at a small practice and qualify as an accountant
Learn each new software tool once it has proved itself
Save for a small house in Marsden

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most. It's too fast for a slow learner, and the shop wouldn't carry us all. What would help is a real first job with a good teacher, family close by, and time to learn without being rushed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that we were told to go to university and it would all be fine. Some of us would rather have had a trade. I'd like young people to be told the truth about that.

headlineQuote: We were told to go to university and it would all be fine. Some of us would rather have had a trade.
portrait: Tomas is a 23-year-old accounting graduate living above his parents' **hardware shop** in Marsden.
He passed with no internship, owes a loan and keeps the shop's **books** by hand and in the computer.
He is traditional and resistant: faith, family and **apprenticeship** matter to him, and he has never used AI.
He stays anxious in most pictures and becomes **alarmed** at the 2-year warning.
His fallback is the shop and its suppliers, but it would not carry the whole family.
biggestWorry: He worries most about **AGI by 2028**, because he is slow with new tools and the shop could not carry everyone.
whatWouldHelp: A real first job with a **good teacher** and time to learn without being rushed.
**Family** close by and honesty about trades.
